claim: Within a bacterial species, genomes separated by larger mutational distances exhibit stronger evidence of purifying selection as assessed by dN/dS.
source: Even within a bacterial species, genomes separated by larger mutational distances exhibit stronger evidence of purifying selection as assessed by dN/dS, the normalized ratio of nonsynonymous to synonymous mutations.
evidence: This is a general observation stated in the abstract that sets up the main research question.

claim: The classical interpretation of dN/dS scale dependence is weak purifying selection.
source: Here, we show that the classical interpretation of this scale dependence, weak purifying selection, leads to problematic mutation accumulation when applied to available gut microbiome data.
evidence: The manuscript states this as the classical interpretation that they are challenging.

claim: The classical weak purifying selection model leads to problematic mutation accumulation when applied to gut microbiome data.
source: Here, we show that the classical interpretation of this scale dependence, weak purifying selection, leads to problematic mutation accumulation when applied to available gut microbiome data.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study demonstrated through analytical and simulation approaches.

claim: Reversions that occur and sweep within-host populations are nearly guaranteed in microbiomes due to large population sizes, short generation times, and variable environments.
source: Reversions that occur and sweep within-host populations are nearly guaranteed in microbiomes due to large population sizes, short generation times, and variable environments.
evidence: This claim is supported by theoretical calculations and simulations presented in the manuscript.

claim: Adaptive reversion can explain the dN/dS decay given only dozens of locally fluctuating selective pressures.
source: Using analytical and simulation approaches, we show that adaptive reversion can explain the dN/dS decay given only dozens of locally fluctuating selective pressures, which is realistic in the context of Bacteroides genomes.
evidence: This is demonstrated through model fitting and simulations in the Results section.

claim: Low values of dN/dS obtained from long timescales may emerge even when adaptive sweeps are frequent.
source: The success of the adaptive reversion model argues for interpreting low values of dN/dS obtained from long timescales with caution as they may emerge even when adaptive sweeps are frequent.
evidence: This is a key conclusion from the reversion model presented in the manuscript.

claim: The vast majority of possible mutations do not increase bacterial fitness and instead result in a neutral or deleterious effect.
source: However, the vast majority of possible mutations do not increase bacterial fitness and instead result in a neutral or deleterious effect (Kimura, 1977; Davies et al., 1999; Jolley et al., 2000; Dingle et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: A dN/dS ratio of >1 indicates the dominance of past adaptive evolution.
source: A dN/dS ratio of >1 indicates the dominance of past adaptive evolution (i.e., directional selection) while a ratio of <1 traditionally implies past selection against amino acid change (purifying selection).
evidence: This is a standard interpretation in population genetics.

claim: A dN/dS ratio of <1 traditionally implies past selection against amino acid change (purifying selection).
source: A dN/dS ratio of >1 indicates the dominance of past adaptive evolution (i.e., directional selection) while a ratio of <1 traditionally implies past selection against amino acid change (purifying selection).
evidence: This is a standard interpretation in population genetics.

claim: Early sequencing work comparing bacterial genomes of the same species reported relatively low dN/dS values across the whole genome (<0.15).
source: Early sequencing work comparing bacterial genomes of the same species reported relatively low dN/dS values across the whole genome (<0.15) (Jolley et al., 2000; Dingle et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: High dN/dS values (~1) were found between closely related strains as sequencing of organisms separated by fewer mutations became feasible.
source: However, as it became economically feasible to sequence organisms separated by fewer mutations and therefore less evolutionary time, a contrasting pattern emerged in which high dN/dS values (~1) were found between closely related strains (Feil et al., 2003; Baker et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Recent work in the human microbiome has found values of dN/dS > 1.
source: Recent work in the human microbiome has confirmed such results and furthered the contrast between timescales by finding values of dN/dS > 1 (Garud et al., 2019; Lieberman et al., 2011; Shoemaker et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent published studies.

claim: The timescale dependence of dN/dS has been mainly attributed to the ongoing action of purifying selection.
source: The timescale dependence of dN/dS has been mainly attributed to the ongoing action of purifying selection (Garud et al., 2019), a model first proposed by Rocha et al., 2006.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Fitting observed data from Garud et al., 2019 with purifying selection yields median values of α ≈ 0.10 (0.09–0.14) and s ≈ 3.5 × 10-5 (2.6 × 10-5-6.5 × 10–5) across all species.
source: Fitting the data from Garud et al., 2019, we infer median values of α ≈ 0.10 (0.09–0.14) and s ≈ 3.5 × 10-5 (2.6 × 10-5-6.5 × 10–5) across all species ('Methods', Figure 1a).
evidence: This is a direct result from fitting the purifying selection model to empirical data.

claim: The purifying selection model indicates that only ~10% of nonsynonymous mutations are neutral and the remaining ~90% are weakly deleterious.
source: These values indicate a model in which only ~10% of nonsynonymous mutations are neutral and the remaining ~90% are so weakly deleterious that they are beyond the limit of detection of any experimental method to date (s ≳ 10–3) (Gallet et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the fitted parameter values from the purifying selection model.

claim: Deep mutational scanning experiments have revealed that most amino acid-changing mutations in essential genes are deleterious enough to be measured in the lab.
source: While the implied proportion of deleterious mutations may seem high, deep mutational scanning experiments have revealed that most amino acid-changing mutations in essential genes are deleterious enough to be measured in the lab (Kelsic et al., 2016; Dewachter et al., 2023); complex real-world environments are expected to constrain an even larger fraction of the genome.
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: With UN/s = 29, the frequency of mutation-free organisms in a population is extremely small (<10–12 after 100,000 generations).
source: With this value of the mutation-selection balance parameter, the frequency of mutation-free organisms in a population is extremely small, even for a population that starts without any deleterious mutations (<10–12 after 100,000 generations).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction from the mutation-selection balance parameter.

claim: Simulations substantiate the prediction of mutation accumulation and decrease in frequency of the wild type under the purifying selection model.
source: Simulations substantiate this prediction of mutation accumulation and decrease in frequency of the wild type (Figure 2a, 'Methods').
evidence: This is demonstrated through computational simulations.

claim: The purifying model requires levels of drift unrealistic at the within-person or across-globe scales.
source: Thus, the purifying model requires levels of drift unrealistic at the within-person or across-globe scales.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the Ne requirements compared to realistic population sizes.

claim: Within-host adaptive sweeps have been observed in Bacteroides fragilis.
source: Lastly, the intolerance of the purifying model to adaptation and transmission is particularly problematic. Within-host adaptive sweeps have been observed in Bacteroides fragilis (Zhao et al., 2019) and other Bacteroides (Garud et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Homologous recombination occurs at detectable rates within human gut microbiomes and within the Bacteroidales order.
source: Homologous recombination, which occurs at detectable rates within human gut microbiomes and within the Bacteroidales order (Liu and Good, 2024), cannot rescue a population from Muller's ratchet when such weakly deleterious mutations are so frequent.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Recombination cannot rescue a population from Muller's ratchet when weakly deleterious mutations are frequent.
source: Homologous recombination, which occurs at detectable rates within human gut microbiomes and within the Bacteroidales order (Liu and Good, 2024), cannot rescue a population from Muller's ratchet when such weakly deleterious mutations are so frequent.
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulations in the manuscript.

claim: Adaptive nonsense mutations have been observed to emerge frequently within individual people in both pathogens and commensals.
source: Adaptive nonsense mutations have been observed to emerge frequently within individual people in both pathogens (Culyba and Van Tyne, 2021; Lieberman et al., 2011; Key et al., 2023; Shopsin et al., 2008) and commensals (Zhao et al., 2019; Barreto et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published studies.

claim: Reversions of stop codons have been observed in mouse models.
source: despite this difficulty, reversions of stop codons have been observed in mouse models (Sousa et al., 2017) and during an outbreak of a pathogen infecting the lungs of people with cystic fibrosis (Poret et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Among the 325 observed nonsynonymous de novo mutations in a study of within-host B. fragilis adaptation, 28 were premature stop codons.
source: Among the 325 observed nonsynonymous de novo mutations in a study of within-host B. fragilis adaptation (Zhao et al., 2019), 28 were premature stop codons.
evidence: This is data extracted from a published study.

claim: The frequency of premature stop codons in B. fragilis de novo mutations is significantly higher than expected by chance (p=0.015).
source: This frequency is significantly higher than expected by chance (p=0.015; 'Methods').
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of the observed data.

claim: A single species within the gut microbiome can have a census population size of 1013.
source: A single species within the gut microbiome can have a census population size of 1013, with generation rates ranging from 1 to 10 per day (Sender et al., 2016; Korem et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Gut microbiome bacteria have generation rates ranging from 1 to 10 per day.
source: A single species within the gut microbiome can have a census population size of 1013, with generation rates ranging from 1 to 10 per day (Sender et al., 2016; Korem et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Given a mutation rate of 10–9 per site per generation, we anticipate 10 mutants at any given site each generation in gut microbiome populations.
source: Given a mutation rate of 10–9 per site per generation, we anticipate 10 mutants at any given site each generation.
evidence: This is calculated from the mutation rate and population size.

claim: Beneficial mutations with sben > 1% generally sweep within 10 years in gut microbiome populations.
source: In the large population sizes relevant for the gut microbiome, a beneficial mutation will then take substantially longer to sweep the population than occur, with values of sben > 1% generally sweeping within 10 years (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is calculated from theoretical models and shown in the figure.

claim: Bacteroidetes genomes are known to have dozens of invertible promoters (up to 47 in B. fragilis).
source: While 55 loci under distinct selective pressures may seem high, Bacteroidetes genomes are known to have dozens of invertible promoters (up to 47 in B. fragilis; Jiang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Adaptive loss-of-function mutations reported in B. fragilis affect the same genes regulated by invertible promoters.
source: Interestingly, adaptive loss-of-function mutations reported in B. fragilis affect the same genes regulated by invertible promoters (Zhao et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Even when the true genome-wide dN/dS exceeds 1, the observed value can be close to 0.1 on long timescales due to reversions.
source: A critical consequence of the reversion model is that apparent and actual dN/dS values diverge quickly. Even when the true genome-wide dN/dS exceeds 1 – meaning that adaptive sweeps have been a dominant force in shaping genomes – the observed value can be close to 0.1 on long timescales.
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulations in the manuscript.

claim: PAML significantly underestimates actual dN/dS when reversion is rampant.
source: We confirmed the inability to detect adaptive selection on a gene when reversion is rampant by simulating protein phylogenies; even the advanced software PAML (Phylogenetic Analysis by Maximum Likelihood) (Yang, 2007) significantly underestimates actual dN/dS (Figure 4b; 'Methods').
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulations testing PAML software.

claim: Specific COG categories in B. fragilis are enriched in TTA and TCA codons relative to baseline, including genes associated with transcription and cell envelope biogenesis.
source: However, specific Clusters of Orthologous Genes (COG) categories are enriched in TTA and TCA codons relative to this baseline, including genes associated with transcription and cell envelope biogenesis (Figure 4c, 'Methods', Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a result from genomic analysis of codon usage.

claim: Genes involved in inorganic ion transport and metabolism that are localized to the outer membrane show enrichment in stop-codon adjacent codons.
source: Further, when functionally annotated genes are further categorized by cellular localization, more gene categories exhibit enrichment (Figure 4c, 'Methods', Supplementary file 1), most notably genes involved in inorganic ion transport and metabolism that are localized to the outer membrane.
evidence: This is a result from genomic analysis of codon usage.

claim: Genes implicated in within-host B. fragilis adaptation are found disproportionately in the category of outer membrane transporters (p=1.22 × 10–4).
source: Genes implicated in within-host B. fragilis adaptation (Zhao et al., 2019) are also found disproportionately in this category of outer membrane transporters (p=1.22 × 10–4; 'Methods', Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis of genomic data.

claim: The cell envelope and membrane-bound transporters are known to mediate interactions with the immune system and phage.
source: Both the cell envelope and membrane-bound transporters are known to mediate interactions with the immune system and phage (Sukhithasri et al., 2013; Ongenae et al., 2022), and are therefore expected to experience fluctuating selective pressures.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Reversions have been relatively overlooked in previous literature because most population genetics theory focuses on eukaryotic organisms with smaller population sizes and longer generation times.
source: It is perhaps not surprising that reversions have been relatively overlooked in previous literature. First, most population genetics theory focuses on eukaryotic organisms with smaller population sizes and longer generation times, for which reversion is less likely.
evidence: This is an explanation for why reversions have not been widely considered.

claim: The infinite-site model assumes that reversions never occur.
source: The low likelihood of reversion in these populations has inspired the use of the convenient infinite-site model (Tajima, 1996), which assumes that reversions never occur and simplifies derivations.
evidence: This is a description of a standard population genetics model.

claim: Theoretical work modeling gut microbiome biogeography suggests that the census and active population sizes differ only approximately tenfold.
source: While gut microbiomes do have a spatial structure that reduces competition, theoretical work modeling this biogeography suggests that the census and active population sizes differ only approximately tenfold (Ghosh and Good, 2022; Labavić et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published theoretical studies.

claim: A recent study tracking de novo mutations between mothers and infants revealed several cases of apparent reversion, with elevated values of dN/dS > 1.
source: Despite this challenge in observation, a recent study tracking de novo mutations between mothers and infants revealed several cases of apparent reversion, with elevated values of dN/dS > 1, though not significantly so (Chen and Garud, 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Many short-term studies in the gut microbiome have revealed strong evidence of within-person adaptation, including parallel evolution.
source: Moreover, many short-term studies in the gut microbiome and beyond have revealed strong evidence of within-person adaptation, including parallel evolution (Lieberman et al., 2011; Marvig et al., 2015; Zhao et al., 2019; Cooper and Lenski, 2000) and loss-of-function changes like premature stop codons (Key et al., 2023) – with low long-term dN/dS values in these same short-term genes (Vigué and Tenaillon, 2023).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published studies.

claim: Data was obtained from Shoemaker et al., 2022 and was initially generated by Garud et al., 2019.
source: Data was obtained from Shoemaker et al., 2022 and was initially generated by Garud et al., 2019.
evidence: This describes the source of the empirical data used in the study.

claim: The parameters for the purifying selection model are estimated using scipy.optimize.curve_fit.
source: The parameters are estimated using scipy.optimize.curve_fit.
evidence: This describes the computational method used for parameter estimation.

claim: The fit minimizes the RMSD of the logarithmic dN/dS.
source: The fit minimizes the RMSD of the logarithmic dN/dS.
evidence: This describes the fitting procedure used in the analysis.

claim: The 10 species analyzed were chosen based on having the most data points reflecting short divergence times (dS < 0.0005).
source: We analyzed the 10 species with the most data points reflecting short divergence times (dS < 0.0005), which is critical for data fit.
evidence: This describes the data selection criteria for the analysis.
